nameStory: The 'shining' in this millipede's name comes from its glossy, polished appearance that catches light beautifully when you spot one crawling through leaf litter. The scientific name 'nantahala' refers to the Nantahala Mountains where this species was first discovered, though it has since been found as far north as New England.
description: The Nantahala shining quick millipede is a small, glossy millipede that moves with surprising speed compared to its larger, slower cousins. These tiny arthropods typically measure only 8-15mm long and have a distinctly shiny, dark brown to black body that looks almost wet. Unlike the chunky garden millipedes most people know, these are slender and quick-moving, with relatively long legs for their size.

idTips.label: Glossy shine
idTips.description: The body has a distinctive wet, polished appearance that reflects light noticeably, even in dim forest conditions

idTips.label: Quick movement
idTips.description: Moves much faster than typical millipedes when disturbed, with a scurrying motion rather than the usual slow crawl

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Only about half an inch long at most, much smaller than the common garden millipedes people usually encounter

idTips.label: Slender build
idTips.description: Body is noticeably thinner and more delicate-looking than chunky pill millipedes, with a cylindrical but streamlined shape

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Deep brown to black color that contrasts sharply with the bright shine, making it stand out against pale leaf litter

habitat: Look for these millipedes in mature deciduous and mixed forests with rich, moist soil and thick leaf litter layers. They prefer areas with good moisture retention under logs, stones, and deep organic matter, particularly in hillier terrain. In New England, they're most likely found in undisturbed forest floors at various elevations.

seasonality.spring: Active as soil warms up, often found under logs and stones during spring cleanup of leaf litter. This is when they're most likely to be moving around visibly.
seasonality.summer: Present but may be deeper in soil or under cover during hot, dry periods. Look in consistently moist microhabitats.
seasonality.fall: Good time to spot them as they prepare for winter, often found in fresh leaf litter accumulations.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in soil or under insulating debris, rarely visible unless you dig through organic layers on warmer days.

funFact: Despite being called millipedes, even the largest members of this group have far fewer than 1,000 legs - and these tiny shining quick millipedes typically have only about 30 pairs of legs, making them more like 'sixty-pedes'!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small centipedes, but remember that millipedes have two pairs of legs per body segment while centipedes have one pair, and millipedes curl up defensively while centipedes try to run away or bite.
contextualKnowledge: The order name 'Chordeumatida' comes from Greek words meaning 'string body,' referring to their thread-like appearance compared to bulkier millipede groups. This is one of the least studied millipede groups in New England, so finding one is genuinely noteworthy for local biodiversity records.
compareHints: Since this is the only Cleidogona species reliably recorded in New England, compare it to other small millipedes in the region by looking for the distinctive glossy shine and quick movement. Most other small millipedes in New England are duller in appearance and move more slowly, lacking that characteristic wet-look shine that makes this species so distinctive.
